title: The Thirty Pieces of Silver
lead: Thirty shekels of silver was the price the law set for a slave killed by an ox (Exodus 21:32). In Zechariah 11:12-13 a shepherd is paid that sum as his wages and throws it to the potter in the house of the LORD. Matthew 26:15 and 27:3-10 tell how the chief priests paid Judas thirty silver coins, how he threw them into the sanctuary, and how they bought the Potter's Field with them, and Matthew names the prophet as Jeremiah.

sections.h: The price of a slave and a shepherd's wage
sections.b: The sum is an insult in the law (Exodus 21:32) and an insult in Zechariah 11:12-13, where the prophet, playing the shepherd of the LORD's flock, asks for his pay and is given 'thirty shekels of silver.' The LORD tells him to throw it 'to the potter,' and the prophet throws it 'into the house of the LORD.' The Greek has 'furnace' for 'potter,' and the Syriac 'treasury'; the Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

sections.h: Judas, the priests and the field
sections.b: Matthew has the chief priests weigh out thirty silver coins to Judas (Matthew 26:15), Judas throw them into the sanctuary (Matthew 27:5), and the priests buy the Potter's Field with 'the price of blood' as a graveyard for strangers (Matthew 27:6-8). He then writes that the word 'spoken through Jeremiah the prophet' was fulfilled (Matthew 27:9-10). The quotation is mostly Zechariah 11:12-13, with the potter's house of Jeremiah 18 and the field bought in Jeremiah 32. Acts 1:18-19 tells the story of the field differently, ending in the name Akeldama, 'Field of Blood.'
